summary: Describes several ways for a Mobile Access Gateway in Proxy Mobile IPv6 to dynamically discover a Local Mobility Anchor, reducing the need for static configuration in large deployments. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: When a phone or other mobile device joins a network, the gateway that handles it needs to find the anchor server that keeps that device's session. This memo lists five ways to do that without configuring every anchor address by hand, and recommends the one that fits any kind of network.

questions: how does a mobile access gateway find an lma
what is a local mobility anchor
subtitle: Ways for a Proxy Mobile IPv6 gateway to find the right mobility anchor automatically instead of by static configuration.

tldr.problem: A gateway that handles mobile nodes has to know which mobility anchor serves each one, and in a large deployment that list is too big to configure by hand.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes five ways to find the anchor: get its address or its name from the AAA server during authentication, build the name from the node's identity or from the service it asked for, or take it from the signalling below IP, then look the name up in DNS.
tldr.outcome: The document recommends the AAA-based approach with fully qualified domain names, because it works the same way across different technologies, and it explains how a handover can still reach the anchor the node already uses.

today: RFC 6097 is an Informational document from February 2011, and the unit metadata records no RFC that obsoletes it and none that updates it. It recommends the AAA-based approach with fully qualified domain names, and leaves the choice of which solution a deployment uses to the operators running it.

sections.title: Why a Gateway Needs to Find an Anchor
sections.content:
A Proxy Mobile IPv6 (RFC 5213) deployment benefits from a function where a Mobile Access Gateway (MAG) can dynamically discover a Local Mobility Anchor (LMA) for a Mobile Node (MN) attaching to a PMIPv6 domain. The purpose of the dynamic discovery function is to reduce the amount of static configuration in the MAG. Other drivers for the dynamic discovery of an LMA include LMA load balancing solutions and selecting an LMA based on desired services, that is, allowing service-specific routing of traffic (RFC 5149).

The document describes several possible dynamic LMA discovery approaches and makes a recommendation of the preferred one. The approaches discussed do not include all possible discovery mechanisms, but are limited to those considered to fit most simply into the PMIPv6 environment. They are: the LMA address is retrieved from the Authentication, Authorization and Accounting (AAA) infrastructure during the network access authentication procedure when the MN attaches to the MAG; the LMA Fully Qualified Domain Name (FQDN) is retrieved from the AAA infrastructure during network access authentication, followed by a DNS lookup; the LMA FQDN is derived from the MN identity received from the lower layers during network attachment, followed by a DNS lookup; the LMA FQDN or IP address is received from the lower layers during network attachment, where reception of an FQDN is followed by a DNS lookup; and the LMA FQDN is derived from the service selection indication received from the lower layers during network attachment, followed by a DNS lookup.

When an MN performs a handover from one MAG to another, the new MAG must use the same LMA that the old MAG was using, because the session has to stay continuous. The discovery mechanism in the new MAG should return the information of the same LMA that the old MAG was using.
sections.plainLanguage: Every mobile session lives on an anchor server. A gateway that has to keep a list of those servers by hand stops being manageable once there are many of them, so the gateway should be able to look one up when a device joins. The document narrows the many possible ways down to five and looks at each.

sections.title: Discovery Through the AAA Infrastructure
sections.content:
This solution requires a MAG to be connected to an AAA infrastructure, as described for instance in RFC 5779, and the AAA infrastructure is assumed to be aware of PMIPv6. A mobile node attaching to a PMIPv6 domain is typically required to provide authentication for network access and to be authorized for mobility services before it is allowed to send or receive any IP packets, or even to complete its IP level configuration.

The AAA-based discovery hooks into the network access authentication and authorization process. The MAG also has the role of a Network Access Server at this step. While the node is attaching to the network, the PMIPv6-related parameters are bootstrapped in parallel with authentication for network access and authorization for mobility services, involving the policy profile download over the AAA infrastructure to the MAG.

In the first variant, after the node has been successfully authenticated for network access and authorized for the mobility service, the MAG receives the LMA IP address from the AAA server over the AAA infrastructure. The address is part of the AAA message that ends the successful authentication and authorization portion of the exchange. Once it has the address, the MAG sends a Proxy Binding Update (PBU) message for the newly authenticated and authorized node. The MAG expects that the LMA returned by the AAA server is able to provide mobility session continuity, so that after a handover the LMA is the same one the node already has a session with.

In the second variant, the procedure is the same except that the MAG receives an FQDN for the LMA instead of the IP address, and has to query DNS to resolve it. The FQDN might be a generic name for a PMIPv6 domain that resolves to one or more LMAs, or it might resolve to exactly one LMA within the domain. The second case is useful if a new target MAG, after a handover, resolves the FQDN to the LMA where the node's session already is.

The two procedures may also be used together. The AAA server might return a generic LMA FQDN during the initial attachment, and once the LMA has been selected, return the LMA IP address during subsequent attachments to other MAGs. For that to work, the resolved and selected LMA IP address must be updated to the remote policy store, which the LMA could do using the AAA infrastructure once it receives the initial PBU.
sections.plainLanguage: The AAA server already has to authenticate the device before it is allowed to send any packets, so the natural place to say which anchor to use is that same exchange. The server can hand over the anchor's address, or a name that the gateway then looks up in DNS. The two can be mixed: a generic name on the first join, the exact address on later joins.

sections.title: Discovery From the Layers Below IP
sections.content:
The remaining solutions are for a MAG that acquires information from layers below the IP layer. Based on that information the MAG can determine which LMA to contact when the node attaches. The lower layers discussed here are not explicitly defined, but include different radio access technologies and tunnelling solutions such as an IKEv2 (RFC 5996) IPsec tunnel (RFC 4303).

The first solution builds the name from the node's identity. A MAG acquires an MN identity from the lower layers and uses information embedded in it to construct a generic LMA FQDN, based on pre-configured formatting rules, and then resolves the LMA IP address using DNS. The identity must embed information that can be used to uniquely identify the entity hosting and operating the LMA for the node. Examples of such identities are the International Mobile Subscriber Identity (IMSI) and the Globally Unique Temporary User Equipment Identity (GUTI), which contain information that can uniquely identify the operator to whom the subscription belongs.

The second solution takes the name or the address straight from the lower layers, for example as part of the normal lower-layer signalling when the node attaches. IKEv2 is an existing example of such signalling where IPsec is the lower layer for the node. IKEv2 has an IKEv2 Identification - Responder (IDr) payload, used by the IKEv2 initiator, which is the node in this case, to specify which of the responder's identities, the LMA in this case, it wants to talk to. The responder identity could be an FQDN or an IP address of the LMA. Another existing example is the Access Point Name Information Element used in 3GPP radio network access signalling and capable of carrying an FQDN. In general this means the node is also the originator of the LMA information, and the content can be transparent to the node, so the node does not associate the information with any LMA function.

The third solution builds the name from a service name. Some network access technologies, including tunnelling solutions, allow the node to signal the service name that identifies a particular service or the external network it wants to reach. If the node-originated service name also embeds the information of the entity hosting the service, or that information can be derived from other information available at the same time, the MAG can construct a generic LMA FQDN providing access to the service or the external network. The pre-defined formatting rules are usually agreed among operators that belong to the same inter-operator roaming consortium, or by network infrastructure vendors defining an open networking system architecture. An example of such a service or external network name is the Access Point Name, which contains the information of the operator providing access to the given service or external network. For example, an FQDN for an ims APN could be ims.apn.epc.mnc015.mcc234.3gppnetwork.org.
sections.plainLanguage: Three more routes start below IP. The node's own identity says which operator it belongs to, so a name can be built from it. The signalling that carries the node onto the network may already name the anchor it wants to reach. Or the service the node asked for names the operator, and the name follows from that. Each of these still ends in a DNS lookup.

sections.title: Keeping the Same Anchor Across a Handover
sections.content:
Whenever a node moves and attaches to a new MAG in a PMIPv6 domain, all the MAGs that the node attaches to should use the same LMA. If there is only one LMA per PMIPv6 domain, there is no issue. If a context transfer mechanism is available between the MAGs, the new MAG knows the LMA information from the old MAG, and such a mechanism is described in RFC 5949. If the node-related context is not transferred between the MAGs, a mechanism is required to deliver the current LMA information to the new MAG.

Relying on DNS during handovers is not generally a working solution if the PMIPv6 domain has more than one LMA, unless the DNS consistently assigns a specific LMA for each given node. In most cases where the MAG derives the LMA FQDN, there is no prior knowledge of whether the FQDN resolves to one or more LMA IP addresses in the domain. Depending on the deployment and deployment-related regulations, such as inter-operator roaming consortium agreements, the situation might not be this desperate. For example, a MAG might be able to synthesize an LMA-specific FQDN out of a node identity or other service-specific parameters. Alternatively the MAG could use a node identity as an input to an algorithm that deterministically assigns the same LMA out of a pool of LMAs, assuming the MAG has, for example, learned a group of LMA FQDNs via an SRV query (RFC 2782). These approaches would guarantee that DNS always returns the same LMA address to the MAG.

Once the node completes its initial attachment to a PMIPv6 domain, the information about the LMA selected to serve it is stored in the policy store, or the AAA server. The LMA conveys that information to the policy store after the initial attachment is completed, and AAA infrastructure is typically used for exchanging information between the LMA and the policy store. When the node moves and attaches to another MAG in the domain, the AAA server delivers the existing LMA information to the new MAG as part of the authentication and authorization procedure.
sections.plainLanguage: A handover only works if the new gateway uses the anchor the old one was using. The document lists three ways to make that happen: there is only one anchor anyway, the gateways hand the information to each other, or the AAA server remembers the choice and tells the new gateway during authentication. Using DNS alone is unreliable unless the name always resolves to the same anchor.

sections.title: What the Document Recommends
sections.content:
All the approaches discussed require additional functionality or infrastructure support that the base PMIPv6 specification (RFC 5213) does not require.

The solutions in the section on discovery from lower layers all depend on the lower layers being able to provide information that a MAG can use to query DNS and discover a suitable LMA. The capabilities of the lower layers and the interactions with them are generally out of the scope of the IETF, and specific to a certain system and architecture.

The solutions in the AAA section depend on the existence of an AAA infrastructure able to provide a MAG with either an LMA IP address or an LMA FQDN. While there can be system- and architecture-specific details regarding the AAA interactions and the use of DNS, the dynamic LMA discovery can be implemented in an access- and technology-agnostic manner, and work in the same way across heterogeneous environments. Using AAA-based LMA discovery solutions is therefore recommended by the document. Furthermore, following the guidance in Section 4, Paragraph 4.1 of RFC 1958, the use of FQDNs should be preferred over IP addresses in the context of AAA-based LMA discovery solutions.
sections.plainLanguage: The recommendation is the AAA route, and inside it, names rather than addresses. The reason is portability: a name still resolves if the anchor moves, and the method works the same whether the access network is Ethernet, wireless or something else.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The use of DNS for obtaining the IP address of a mobility agent carries certain security risks, explained in detail in Section 9.1 of RFC 5026. The risks described in RFC 5026 are mitigated to a large extent in this document, since the MAG and the LMA belong to the same PMIPv6 domain, and the DNS server that the MAG queries is also part of the same PMIPv6 domain. Even if the MAG obtains the IP address of a bogus LMA from a bogus DNS server, further harm is prevented because the MAG and the LMA should authenticate each other before exchanging PMIPv6 signalling messages. RFC 5213 specifies the use of IKEv2 between the MAG and the LMA to authenticate each other and set up IPsec security associations for protecting the PMIPv6 signalling messages.

The AAA infrastructure may be used to transport the LMA-discovery-related information between the MAG and the AAA server via one or more AAA brokers and/or AAA proxies. In that case, the MAG-to-AAA-server communication relies on the security properties of the intermediate AAA brokers and AAA proxies.
sections.plainLanguage: A poisoned name lookup is not fatal here, because the gateway and the anchor still authenticate each other with IKEv2 before they exchange anything. What remains in the operator's hands is the security of the AAA brokers in between.

messages.note: The gateway asks the AAA server to authenticate the node and authorize it for mobility.

messages.note: The AAA server returns the anchor address, or a name to look up in DNS.

messages.note: The gateway registers the new session with the anchor.

viz.caption: THE FIVE WAYS TO FIND THE ANCHOR

items.title: AAA returns the address
items.text: The anchor's IP address arrives with the successful authentication and authorization message.

items.title: AAA returns the name
items.text: The anchor's fully qualified domain name arrives instead, and the gateway looks it up in DNS.

items.title: The node's identity gives the name
items.text: The identity names the operator, so the gateway builds a name from it and looks it up.

items.title: The lower layers supply it
items.text: Signalling below IP already names the anchor the node wants to reach.

items.title: The service name gives the name
items.text: The service the node asked for names the operator, and the name follows from that.

viz.caption: HOW THE NEW GATEWAY LEARNS WHICH ANCHOR THE NODE ALREADY USES

cells: Every gateway already knows it, so there is nothing to look up
The new gateway is handed the anchor information by the old one
The server stores the chosen anchor and passes it to the new gateway at authentication
DNS with a consistent per-node answer
The name always resolves to the same anchor for that node
